claims.text: Conventional unmodified W–Cu composites exhibit relatively low thermal conductivity because of high electron scattering at W/Cu boundaries.
Depositing a uniform, ultra-thin nickel layer on tungsten surfaces before copper infiltration or consolidation will create a Ni interphase at W–Cu interfaces.
A Ni interphase is chemically compatible with W–Cu interfaces and acts as an interfacial binder.
The Ni interphase promotes coherent bonding at W–Cu interfaces.
The Ni interphase reduces mismatch in electron density and phonon spectra across W–Cu interfaces.
Reduced electronic and vibrational mismatch minimizes electron scattering and interfacial thermal resistance.
A nanoscale Ni layer enhances electron transmission across the W–Cu interface.
Enhanced electron transmission reduces interfacial thermal resistance and increases the composite's overall thermal conductivity.
Nickel has sufficient inherent mechanical strength to support the composite's durability.
Nickel has sufficient irradiation stability to limit irradiation-induced microstructural damage in the composite.
Relative to an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite, the Ni-coated composite will exhibit a statistically measurable increase in thermal conductivity.
The Ni-coated composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to or better than the unmodified control.
The Ni-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to or better than the unmodified control.
The predicted benefit applies at elevated operating temperatures of approximately 500–1000 °C under irradiation conditions representative of fusion-reactor joints.
The hypothesis is limited to a uniform Ni interphase thinner than 10 nm.
A Ni coating that is too thick or discontinuous may not provide the predicted benefits.
The long-term stability of the Ni interphase under extended irradiation and cyclic thermal loading is unresolved.
